cells.why: Open, as PD's cell. The memory rung and the tier do not change a `persisted` write. E-22 showed the pattern on fero's library shape, not on PD's kernel commands, 2PC and oracle. The native bar is C + 0.5 ms = 1.23 ms: E-02's Rust pipeline reads p99 0.67 ms with separate disks emulated and 1.58 ms on this one shared disk, so this box cannot settle it. A 2PC write also asks the oracle for a timestamp, one more round trip (58 us p99 in Rust on loopback, E-01): it fits the bar but was not run. The LSM write path was never timed. A held row reads in 81 ns on the client (E-44).

Open. etcd here: 1,118 puts a second at one client (p99 1.73 ms) and 22,800 at 1,000 clients (E-09e). etcd always fsyncs, so its default row is its matched row and the memory rung is not the matching rung here. The best a `persisted` commit can do on this box is about 0.42 ms p99 with the client's hop (RR-04's sum from E-01), and the oracle's round trip adds about 0.06 to 0.1 ms: both stay under 1.73 ms, so no ceiling stops the row. W `lease` gives a one-hop linearizable range. But no PD-shaped kernel ran behind the etcd gateway, which has only driven a simulator (E-45).

Open, as PD's cell. Native bar 1.23 ms. E-02's Rust pipeline reads p99 0.67 ms with separate disks emulated and 1.58 ms on this one disk, so the box shows the bar neither met nor missed. The LSM write path (Raft log plus applied state) was never timed, and background compaction and the tier's uploads add disk work beside the commit fsync (A-09 asks that bulk writes not starve it). The memory rung does not change a `persisted` commit.

Open. PD failed only because a full disk loss left no copy anywhere (no tier). With the tier a copy exists, so that structural fail goes. Not shown: no sleep and wake ran against an object store, with disks kept or lost; how fast 10 GB comes back from the store into an LSM was never measured (E-28 timed single PUTs only); and the controller's own state (the region table, the oracle's high-water) must come back from the store too. An LSM opens without folding every row, so E-34's Node figure (86 to 122 s for 10 GB) does not bind this native server, as for SRV (reasoned). Both readings of the 1.3 line give open.

Met, as PD's cell (both judges). An LSM holds state larger than memory by construction, and regions spread a resource over servers' disks (TiKV and CockroachDB in production, cited). The tier does not take the LSM away; it adds a copy in the store. A cold read is a local disk read, under one object-store get (about 30 ms on S3, cited in E-28); if old files live only in the store, a cold read is one get. Not measured here. The prediction (open) falls to the draft's 'snapshot layers, by design only' because no judged row holds `lsm +tier`; the option that decides this SHOULD is the LSM, which this row keeps.

Open, as PD's cell. E-35 ran a shared journal, not an LSM. Here a 1 MB record ten times a second is 10 MB a second into the LSM, then flushes, compactions and the tier's uploads, all beside other partitions' commits on the same disk. None of it was measured, and the 1 MB, 64 MB and `too-large` limits were not built.

Open, as PD's referee ruled: a synced write must also come back after a power cut, and this LSM was never power-cut here (E-29 ran its own journal, which still lost a batch in 2 of 1,200 rounds through a recovery bug before its fix). Open in both readings. PD's write, failover and new-replica paths use no object store (PD's cell: met by construction), and the tier only uploads behind them, as KIP-405 does for ISR's segments. Two things could still put the store in a path F-15 does not allow. add.name: The oracle's high-water kept in the store's manifest (a restore starts above it)
add.state: In the object store's manifest: the top of the oracle's current timestamp window (and the id allocator's top), written before the oracle hands out a timestamp of that window; after a restore, the restore's first timestamp, kept as a floor.
add.rules: (1) Before the oracle uses a new window it records the window's top in the store (a conditional write). (2) A restore starts the oracle above that top and above wall time, and records its first timestamp as the floor. (3) A transaction whose start timestamp is below the floor is refused, so a retry from before the restore is refused, not re-run (OPS-07, F-02).
add.precedent: PD's own oracle saves its window's top before use (the settled `timestamp-oracle` unit, not novel by both counters); this is the same state and rule with the store as its home, where A-08 and E-33 put a restore's high-water mark. If the referee reads it as the settled `restore-mark` unit instead (novel: PostgreSQL timelines are the nearest, not the same), the row's novel count is 1 and its pairs rise by 6, not 5.

mechanisms.why: Missing: the oracle's high-water outside the restored data. The settled count leaves PD out of `restore-mark` because 'the oracle saves its high-water before use, outside the data a restore brings back' (MECHANISMS section 4, `restore-mark`). The tier changes that premise. This row now restores from the store (SC-05 wakes servers that lost their disks; OPS-07 restores a project to a past position), and the cheap shape under DEP-21's bar puts the controller inside the stores (RR-06), so the controller's disks, and the oracle's saved window with them, can be lost together with the data. Then a restore that reads the oracle's state from the store's last upload can hand out a timestamp twice: a version or a fence token repeats, which is E-33's R1 and R2 counterexample (5 and 6 steps) in timestamp form. Fence tokens are seen by outside systems, so a new cluster id does not save them. So the row needs either this state (added here: 238 -> 243 pairs, +5: with closed-timestamps, mvcc, tier, timestamp-oracle, two-phase-commit) or a stated clock rule (after a restore the oracle waits out wall time plus the window plus the largest clock skew; no new state, but a reliance on bounded skew that PD's own window save exists to avoid). Not added for a clean sleep alone: there the last upload carries the exact high-water. Checked and not missing: (a) the memory rung on an LSM is the settled `memory-rung` (a clean-stop mark per replica) with RocksDB-style unsynced writes; its 'rejoin as new' must be per group (a new Raft member id, `raft-config`), not per dir (`disk-incarnation`), or one unclean stop wipes the store's `persisted` groups too (K-09, K-24): a rule, no new state. (b) The tier on an LSM uploads sorted files and a per-store manifest, not per-group segments named by a log entry: the same role as `tier` (precedent rocksdb-cloud's files in S3 and TiKV's backup to S3, both from memory, not checked); `tier` should also read `lsm.files`, which adds no pair (it already pairs with `lsm-store` through `durable.log`). (c) `rejoin` on an LSM: `disk-incarnation` per dir means one bad block wipes every region on that store (K-24): safe, costly, no new state. One interaction the pair rule does not see: `memory-rung` and `two-phase-commit` share no listed variable, yet a Percolator unit whose primary or secondary sits in a memory-rung group can be half lost when that group's majority stops uncleanly. It needs one rule (a unit's records commit at `persisted`, or a unit inherits its weakest resource's loss contract). The same holds for COMP's sagas (K-09); the settled P-15 cells of the saga rows with Q `mix` are met, so P-15 is left as predicted here. Novel: none. `memory-rung`, `tier`, `disk-incarnation` and `lsm-store` are settled not novel; the added unit has PD's own oracle as its precedent. So the row stays at 0 novel (1 if the referee counts the added unit as `restore-mark`). Nothing listed is unneeded. Row-specific: `learners`, `route-smart` and `worker-map` (V +lrn, Y smart, M kwN) are PD's and needed. With `rejoin` it carries no `par-repair`, as listed.

Met, by model. Z `par`: a checksum per entry finds the bad entry, and the damaged voter refuses to vote or stand until it copies the entry from a peer that knows it is committed and whose own copy is good. TLC on etcd's spec (`par1`): 62,743 states, all 10 invariants hold, no committed write lost; each of par's 7 rules shown needed by a mutant (E-37). The port runs etcd's raft, which E-37's spec is (E-10).

Repair must come from any peer, not only the leader (`par2d-leader`: 9 % stuck). This is the cell the VERDICT gives COMP2. Same limits as the MUST part: three voters, no membership change, log entries only.

TLC on etcd's spec (`par1`): 62,743 states, all 10 invariants hold, no committed write lost; each of par's 7 rules shown needed by a mutant (E-37). The model also keeps 'takes no append while damaged' as a guard (not needed for safety), so the voter acknowledges nothing on the bad entry. Limits: three voters, no membership change (G-15). E-37's entry is a log entry. In an LSM, entries below the applied index are compacted into sorted files; damage there is found by the store's own block checksums and repaired by a snapshot from a peer, which E-37 did not model. Carried to raft-rs by reasoning, as the RUST and SRV cells carry E-37; Go's etcd raft is the spec's own code. Either core needs par's vote and repair rules added inside it.

Met, by model. `par2d`: one bad entry on each of two replicas at different offsets, 565,222 states, 276 judged two-damage states, 0 stuck (E-37); with the same offset it stays writable whenever a good copy is left (`par2`, the 4 stuck states have no good copy). Repair must come from any peer, not only the leader (`par2d-leader`: 9 % stuck). This is the cell the VERDICT gives COMP2. Same limits as the MUST part: three voters, no membership change, log entries only.

Open, as PD's cell. Nothing of the LSM shape ran here. RocksDB and TiKV's raft engine share one WAL sync among a write group (cited from memory by both PD judges). E-02 and E-12 show group commit on a journal, not on this store. The tier and the memory rung do not change it.

Open, as PD's cell. E-42 costed its recorder on a journal it can point into (1.1 to 1.7 % of a core). Here bulk bytes sit in an LSM that rewrites its own files, and the tier adds object-store completions as inputs, which E-42 never recorded.

Open. PD met it only because nothing held two projects: no object store. The tier puts every project's old data in the hosted object store, which OPS-14 names. Like COMP, SRV and MIN-P (N `proc` with a store): a key per project at rest and no read path across projects are owed (OPS-13), not designed or tested. Servers stay one set per project, so no log-tier budget applies.

add.name: The oracle's high-water kept in the store's manifest (a restore starts above it)
add.state: In the object store's manifest: the top of the oracle's current timestamp window (and the id allocator's top), written before the oracle hands out a timestamp of that window; after a restore, the restore's first timestamp, kept as a floor.
add.rules: (1) Before the oracle uses a new window it records the window's top in the store (a conditional write). (2) A restore starts the oracle above that top and above wall time, and records its first timestamp as the floor. (3) A transaction whose start timestamp is below the floor is refused, so a retry from before the restore is refused, not re-run (OPS-07, F-02).
add.precedent: PD's own oracle saves its window's top before use (the settled `timestamp-oracle` unit, not novel by both counters); this is the same state and rule with the store as its home, where A-08 and E-33 put a restore's high-water mark. If the referee reads it as the settled `restore-mark` unit instead (novel: PostgreSQL timelines are the nearest, not the same), the row's novel count is 1 and its pairs rise by 6, not 5.

mechanisms.why: Missing: the oracle's high-water outside the restored data. The settled count leaves PD out of `restore-mark` because 'the oracle saves its high-water before use, outside the data a restore brings back' (MECHANISMS section 4, `restore-mark`). The tier changes that premise. This row now restores from the store (SC-05 wakes servers that lost their disks; OPS-07 restores a project to a past position), and the cheap shape under DEP-21's bar puts the controller inside the stores (RR-06), so the controller's disks, and the oracle's saved window with them, can be lost together with the data. Then a restore that reads the oracle's state from the store's last upload can hand out a timestamp twice: a version or a fence token repeats, which is E-33's R1 and R2 counterexample (5 and 6 steps) in timestamp form. Fence tokens are seen by outside systems, so a new cluster id does not save them. So the row needs either this state (added here: 214 -> 219 pairs, +5: with closed-timestamps, mvcc, tier, timestamp-oracle, two-phase-commit) or a stated clock rule (after a restore the oracle waits out wall time plus the window plus the largest clock skew; no new state, but a reliance on bounded skew that PD's own window save exists to avoid). Not added for a clean sleep alone: there the last upload carries the exact high-water. Checked and not missing: (a) the memory rung on an LSM is the settled `memory-rung` (a clean-stop mark per replica) with RocksDB-style unsynced writes; its 'rejoin as new' must be per group (a new Raft member id, `raft-config`), not per dir (`disk-incarnation`), or one unclean stop wipes the store's `persisted` groups too (K-09, K-24): a rule, no new state. (b) The tier on an LSM uploads sorted files and a per-store manifest, not per-group segments named by a log entry: the same role as `tier` (precedent rocksdb-cloud's files in S3 and TiKV's backup to S3, both from memory, not checked); `tier` should also read `lsm.files`, which adds no pair (it already pairs with `lsm-store` through `durable.log`). (c) `rejoin` on an LSM: `disk-incarnation` per dir means one bad block wipes every region on that store (K-24): safe, costly, no new state. One interaction the pair rule does not see: `memory-rung` and `two-phase-commit` share no listed variable, yet a Percolator unit whose primary or secondary sits in a memory-rung group can be half lost when that group's majority stops uncleanly. It needs one rule (a unit's records commit at `persisted`, or a unit inherits its weakest resource's loss contract). The same holds for COMP's sagas (K-09); the settled P-15 cells of the saga rows with Q `mix` are met, so P-15 is left as predicted here. Novel: none. `memory-rung`, `tier`, `disk-incarnation` and `lsm-store` are settled not novel; the added unit has PD's own oracle as its precedent. So the row stays at 0 novel (1 if the referee counts the added unit as `restore-mark`). Nothing listed is unneeded. Row-specific: no memory rung here, so the 2PC interaction and K-09 do not apply. `par` on an LSM as for B1: `par-repair` covers the Raft log, sorted-file damage falls to the store's block checksums and a snapshot from a peer; par's vote and repair rules must be added inside raft-rs or Go's etcd raft (a fork of either). `disk-incarnation` stays (A-01 rule 4).
